Article 2 of the Convention reads as follows: “1.  Everyone’s right to life shall be protected by law. No one shall be deprived of his life intentionally save in the execution of a sentence of a court following his conviction of a crime for which this penalty is provided by law.

concepts.interpretation: Article 2 safeguards the right to life and requires the State to refrain from unlawful taking of life and to take appropriate steps to safeguard lives within its jurisdiction, including positive obligations to prevent suicide in detention.

anchor.surface_text: Article 3 of the Convention ranks as one of the most fundamental provisions in the Convention, to which no derogation is permitted.

concepts.interpretation: Article 3 prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment; the Court applies a particularly thorough scrutiny to allegations under Article 3.

anchor.surface_text: Article 5 of the Convention, the Court has reiterated in that connection that any deprivation of liberty must not only have been effected in conformity with the substantive and procedural rules of national law but must equally be in keeping with the very purpose of Article 5

concepts.interpretation: Article 5 protects against arbitrary detention and requires lawful arrest and prompt judicial control of detention.

anchor.surface_text: Article 6 of the Convention, which, in relevant part, provides as follows: “1.  In the determination ... of any criminal charge against him, everyone is entitled to a fair ... hearing ... 3.  Everyone charged with a criminal offence has the following minimum rights: ... (c)  to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of his own choosing

concepts.interpretation: Article 6 guarantees the right to a fair trial including the right to legal assistance at the preliminary investigation stage depending on the circumstances.

Article 8 reads as follows: “1. Everyone has the right to respect for his private and family life,... 2. There shall be no interference by a public authority with the exercise of this right except such as is in accordance with the law and is necessary in a democratic society ...

concepts.interpretation: Article 8 protects the right to respect for private and family life including the right to communicate with detained relatives; positive obligations may arise.

anchor.surface_text: Article 13 of the Convention provides as follows: “Everyone whose rights and freedoms as set forth in [the] Convention are violated shall have an effective remedy before a national authority notwithstanding that the violation has been committed by persons acting in an official capacity.”

concepts.interpretation: Article 13 requires the availability of an effective domestic remedy to enforce Convention rights including thorough and effective investigations.

anchor.surface_text: Article 14 of the Convention, which provides: “The enjoyment of the rights and freedoms set forth in [the] Convention shall be secured without discrimination on any ground such as sex, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, birth or other status.”

concepts.interpretation: Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of Convention rights.

anchor.surface_text: States have a wide margin of appreciation regarding the choice of the means to be employed to discharge such obligations in relevant legislation (see Zehnalova and Zehnal, cited above).

concepts.interpretation: The Court recognizes a margin of appreciation for States in how they regulate communications between detainees and family.

anchor.surface_text: the Court recalls that, in assessing evidence, it adopts the standard of proof “beyond reasonable doubt” (see Orhan v. Turkey, no. 25656/94, § 264, 18 June 2002).

concepts.interpretation: The Court applies the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt in assessing allegations of violations under Article 2 and 3.

anchor.surface_text: the Court therefore considers that the applicant’s complaints raised arguable claims of violations of the Convention for the purposes of Article 13 of the Convention.

concepts.interpretation: The Court treats complaints as arguable claims under Article 13 even if not proven beyond reasonable doubt, triggering the obligation to investigate.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT UNANIMOUSLY

1.  Holds that there has been no violation of Article 2 of the Convention;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found insufficient evidence beyond reasonable doubt that the applicant's son was killed by State agents or inmates, and no failure to supervise leading to suicide was established. The investigation into the death was adequate and effective.

holdings.text: Holds that there has been no violation of Article 3 of the Convention;

anchor.surface_text: 1.  Holds that there has been no violation of Article 3 of the Convention;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found no evidence of ill-treatment of the applicant's son in police custody and no special factors to establish a violation of Article 3 for the applicant himself.

holdings.text: Holds that there has been no violation of Article 5 of the Convention in respect of the disappearance of the applicant’s son between 5 October and 2 November 1999;

anchor.surface_text: 2.  Holds that there has been no violation of Article 5 of the Convention in respect of the disappearance of the applicant’s son between 5 October and 2 November 1999;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court accepted the Government's position that the kidnappers were not State agents and that the son was not in police custody during that period.

holdings.text: Holds that there has been a violation of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention with respect to the length of the detention of the applicant’s son in police custody;

anchor.surface_text: 3.  Holds that there has been a violation of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention with respect to the length of the detention of the applicant’s son in police custody;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found that the nine-day detention without judicial control exceeded the acceptable limits established in precedent (Brogan and Others v. UK).

holdings.text: Holds that there has been a violation of Article 5 § 5 of the Convention as regards the inability of the applicant’s son to obtain compensation for the excessive length of detention in police custody;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found no enforceable right to compensation existed domestically for the unlawful detention period, constituting a violation of Article 5 § 5.

holdings.text: Holds that there has been no violation of Article 6 of the Convention;

anchor.surface_text: 5.  Holds that there has been no violation of Article 6 of the Convention;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court did not examine the complaint fully as the charges were dropped after the son's death, thus no violation of Article 6 was found.

anchor.surface_text: 7.  Holds that there has been a violation of Article 13 of the Convention in respect of the disappearance and ill‑treatment of the applicant’s son between 5 October and 2 November 1999;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found serious shortcomings in the investigation and lack of effective remedy regarding the disappearance and ill-treatment allegations, constituting a violation of Article 13.

holdings.text: Holds that there has been no violation of Article 14 of the Convention;

anchor.surface_text: 8.  Holds that there has been no violation of Article 14 of the Convention;

holdings.text: Holds that the respondent State is to pay the applicant, within three months from the date on which the judgment becomes final in accordance with Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, the following amounts: (i) EUR 10,500 in respect of non-pecuniary damage; (ii) EUR 2,500 for costs and expenses incurred in respect of Mr İ. Sağlam; (iii) EUR 8,000 for costs and expenses in respect of the applicant’s representatives in the United Kingdom; (iv) any tax that may be chargeable on all the above amounts; and that from the expiry of the above-mentioned three months until settlement simple interest shall be payable on the above amounts at a rate equal to the marginal lending rate of the European Central Bank during the default period plus three percentage points; dismisses the remainder of the applicant’s claim for just satisfaction.
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court awarded just satisfaction for non-pecuniary damage and costs related to legal representation, applying default interest, and dismissed other claims for pecuniary damage due to lack of evidence.

outcome.relief_summary: Violations found of Articles 5 §§ 3 and 5, 8 and 13; no violations of Articles 2, 3, 5 (disappearance), 6, 14, 38; awarded EUR 10,500 non-pecuniary damage; awarded EUR 8,000 and EUR 2,500 for costs and expenses to applicant's representatives in UK and Turkey respectively; remainder of just satisfaction claims dismissed.
